newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices rise after UN predicts Iraq deal delay.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices rise after UN predicts Iraq deal delay.

text.p: World oil prices recovered again on Thursday after a series of sharp losses in the last two weeks amid reports that Iraqi crude oil sales under a U.N. deal might be delayed.
London July futures for world benchmark Brent crude oil closed nine cents a barrel up at $17.44.
Prices fell on Wednesday as low as $17.32 a barrel, the lowest point since May last year and well over three dollars a barrel cheaper than in the middle of last month.
Traders said a lack of follow-through selling on Thursday after the hefty falls indicated the market may have found a resting place for the moment.
"If people had wanted to sell, they would have done so by now," one said.

Antonio Monteiro, chairman of the U.N. sanctions committee on Iraq, said late on Wednesday Baghdad would submit a new pricing formula for oil sales under the oil-for-food deal only after the agreement of a food distribution plan - which U.N. officials said would be completed around the end of the month.

Iraqi crude oil exports have been under U.N. trade sanctions since Iraq's August 1990 invasion of Kuwait but Baghdad was allowed to sell limited oil to buy food and medicines under a renewable six-month deal agreed with the United Nations last December.
The renewed plan came into force on June 8.
"There is certainly a cloud over the deal," said a dealer at London's International Petroleum Exchange.
But others played down the importance of the expected delay to the plan. They said the delay was administrative and not political and therefore still likely to go ahead.

"They have still got the same amount of oil to sell," one broker said. "It just means they have got five months to sell it in, and not six months. We have got so much oil out here to play with - who cares about a delay?"
Against this backdrop lies a picture of a healthy world oil supply.

Some downwards pressure was exerted on prices by news that Germany was considering selling 7.3 million tonnes of crude oil, some 20 percent of its strategic oil reserves, to help plug a hole in government finances. A decision was expected on the sale on July 11.
"Even though it's only 100,000 barrels per day it's another nail in a bearish coffin," said Russell Hill of Austrian oil company OMV.

U.S. weekly industry data released this week also showed stocks of gasoline, which is considered a key marker for energy markets during the summer driving season, were 2.7 million barrels higher than at the same time last week.
